newsitem.title: USA: World Bank to work harder to fight African poverty.
newsitem.headline: World Bank to work harder to fight African poverty.

text.p: Admitting that its efforts toward reducing poverty in Sub-Saharan Africa have been insufficient, the World Bank Wednesday said it must work harder to spur growth in the troubled region.

The Bank, in a report, said the key to improved conditions was the achievement of sustained high growth rates, although to reduce poverty, the growth must target the disadvantaged either directly or through improved social services.
"Growth rates of at least 6.5 percent per year are necessary if typical Sub-Saharan African countries are to reduce poverty at an acceptable rate," the report said.

"But growth alone is insufficient without a pattern of growth that allows for increased production, expanded employment opportunities for the poor and better access to social services for the poorest groups," it added.
The report, however, noted that the Bank's most recent forecast is for growth to increase 3.8 percent per year over the next decade.
It noted that poverty is deeply-rooted in Africa and that its eradication will be extremely difficult.

About 45 percent of the approximately 590 million people in the region live below the national poverty line and at least 50 percent of these live in six countries -- Ethiopia, Kenya, Nigeria, Sudan, Tanzania and Uganda, the report said.
"Progress toward reducing the porportion of people below the poverty line had been unacceptably slow and past efforts insufficient," the Bank said.
It said the bank would focus more on rural development in the poorest areas -- not only on agriculture -- but on water supplies, roads, education and health.

At the same time, it said reducing barriers to trade in an environment of market based-exchange rates will provide incentives for exports while making expensive imports less attractive, improving the situation for poor people.
With this improved structure, food security is strengthened because prices are stabilized, making more food available and affordable for the poor, the Bank said.
